ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, shareholders, and directors against TRACFIN, OFAC, UN, EU consolidated sanctions lists, and the French domestic anti-terrorism list (Fichier des Personnes et Entités Sanctionnées). PEP status (Politically Exposed Persons) must be verified via independent open-source and commercial KYC databases; enhanced due diligence required for PEPs, crypto-related businesses, and high-risk third-country residents. Declaration obligations to TRACFIN apply to any unusual, suspicious, or crypto-arbitrage transactions under Monetary and Financial Code Article L.561-15.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: INPI (Institut National de la Propriété Industrielle) – Registre National des Entreprises (RNE) integrated within the official French business formalities portal (guichet unique, formalites.entreprises.gouv.fr)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The proposed name may be in any language using Latin script, but must be transliterated into French script for official registry publication (if using non-Latin characters). The corporate name must be distinctive and must not conflict with an existing French or EU trademark, protected trade name (nom commercial), or registered company name. The name must respect French public order and good morals. For an SAS, the name is set forth in the Articles of Association (statuts).
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the INPI/RNE rejects the proposed name, the applicant may file a written administrative appeal using the guichet unique portal within 2 (two) months from notification of the rejection (per Code de Commerce Article R.123-36-1). The appeal is directed to the Director-General of INPI. If the administrative appeal is denied, the applicant may bring a judicial appeal before the Paris Court of Appeal (Cour d'appel de Paris) within 1 (one) month of the rejection decision. Alternatively, the applicant may propose a modified name and re-file the pre-incorporation formality.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted for this industry (ISIC 6201 / NAICS 518210). A registered office (siège social) may be designated at (a) a functional physical office or co-working space, or (b) under an approved domiciliation contract (contrat de domiciliation) with an authorized domiciliation company (société de domiciliation). Virtual office agreements are deemed compliant with Article L.123-11 of the Commercial Code provided the agreement includes the provision of a physical mailbox, access to a meeting room, and legal notification service. The commercial activity of data pipeline APIs does not violate domiciliation restrictions; however, the domiciliary company must be registered with the local Prefecture or Greffe.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Quantified risk: 20% annually for an SAS in the data/commerce API sector. Inspections may be conducted without prior notice by the Registrar (Greffe du Tribunal de Commerce) or the National Council of Court Clerks (Conseil National des Greffiers) to verify effective substance, presence of a physical or contractual mailbox, and compliance with the domiciliation contract.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP), administered through the competent Service des impôts des entreprises (SIE); online tax administration portal: impots.gouv.fr. Company formation and business-registration filings are submitted through the Guichet unique operated by the Institut national de la propriété industrielle (INPI).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A French SAS obtains its statutory identifiers through the INPI Guichet unique: (1) file incorporation documents, registered-office evidence, beneficial-owner information, management details, corporate purpose, and capital information; (2) receive a SIREN for the legal entity and a SIRET for each establishment from the national business register; (3) obtain the applicable tax account with the competent SIE; (4) request a French intra-Community VAT identification number through the SIE or the DGFiP professional tax portal; and (5) activate the professional account for VAT returns, payment, correspondence, and electronic filing. A foreign entity without a French establishment must apply to the French non-established taxable-person VAT service, generally the Service des impôts des entreprises étrangères, before or when French VAT obligations arise. The application must identify the legal entity, foreign tax number, activities, French customers or transactions, bank details, representative or correspondence arrangements where required, and evidence of taxable transactions. France does not generally impose a turnover threshold on non-established businesses for VAT registration where France is the place of taxation, subject to reverse-charge and special-regime rules. A foreign entity operating through a French permanent establishment must obtain French business-registration identifiers and register with the SIE assigned to that establishment.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: A SAS is subject to French corporate income tax (impôt sur les sociétés, IS) by default. A qualifying SAS may elect temporarily for partnership-style income taxation (impôt sur le revenu, IR) for a maximum statutory period of five financial years, subject to conditions including qualifying ownership, size, age, activity, and shareholder approval; the election is notified to the competent tax authority within the applicable deadline and is not a general check-the-box election. A family-owned qualifying company may use a separate family-company election where statutory conditions are met. France has no United States-style entity classification check-the-box regime. Hybrid mismatch rules can deny deductions, include income, or restrict treaty and directive benefits where arrangements produce a deduction/non-inclusion, double deduction, or imported mismatch outcome. These rules do not create a general elective tax classification.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Value Added Tax (Taxe sur la valeur ajoutée, VAT)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: For a non-established taxable person making transactions taxable in France, there is generally no de minimis VAT registration threshold: registration is required when a French VAT obligation arises, unless the customer accounts for VAT under a reverse-charge rule or a special regime applies. For French-established businesses eligible for the domestic franchise en base regime, the principal 2025 turnover thresholds are EUR 37,500 for services and EUR 85,000 for supplies of goods, with enhanced thresholds of EUR 41,250 and EUR 93,500 respectively; the regime is subject to statutory conditions, activity-specific rules, and legislative amendments. A business may voluntarily opt for VAT taxation where permitted. The standard French VAT rate is 20%; reduced rates apply only to specifically listed transactions.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: France is implementing mandatory electronic invoicing and transaction e-reporting for businesses established in France. From 1 September 2026, all businesses must be able to receive compliant electronic invoices, and large and medium-sized businesses must issue them electronically; small and micro-businesses are scheduled to issue them from 1 September 2027, subject to the applicable implementation timetable. Invoices must generally pass through an approved private electronic invoicing platform (plateforme agréée), with public-sector invoices continuing through Chorus Pro where applicable. France does not operate a universal real-time invoice-by-invoice fiscal-clearance model comparable to Italy. Required data, invoice status information, and applicable domestic and cross-border transaction data are transmitted to the tax administration through the approved platform and e-reporting channels. Electronic records must preserve authenticity, integrity, readability, auditability, and the statutory retention period. Non-established suppliers may be outside the French e-invoicing mandate unless they have a French establishment or otherwise fall within a covered domestic reporting obligation; their French VAT invoicing and reporting duties remain transaction-specific.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exports of goods dispatched from France to a destination outside the European Union may be invoiced at 0% French VAT where the supplier is the exporter or can prove that the goods left the EU customs territory and the statutory export conditions are satisfied. The supplier must retain a customs export declaration and reliable electronic evidence of exit, normally including the export MRN and the customs exit result or equivalent validated exit evidence. Supplies to an EU member state are generally intra-Community supplies, not third-country exports, and require separate conditions including customer VAT identification and transport evidence. B2B services supplied to a business customer established outside France are generally taxed at the customer’s establishment under the place-of-supply rule and are normally invoiced without French VAT, subject to use-and-enjoyment, immovable-property, event, transport, intermediary, and other special rules. Automated data, scraping, proxy, and API services require transaction-by-transaction classification; B2B supplies to a foreign business generally follow the B2B rule, while B2C supplies may be subject to French VAT or an EU special regime depending on customer location and the electronically supplied-service rules. Export zero-rating or exemption must be supported by contemporaneous commercial, contractual, transport, customs, and payment records. VAT refunds require valid input VAT invoices, business-purpose evidence, non-exempt taxable activity, and compliance with the applicable French or EU refund procedure.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Commercial invoice identifying the supplier, customer, goods, value, delivery terms, and zero-rating basis
French export customs declaration containing the export MRN and accurate commodity, value, origin, exporter, and consignee data
Electronic customs exit evidence, such as the Export Accompanying Document and validated exit result or equivalent customs exit message
Transport evidence, such as bill of lading, air waybill, consignment note, carrier proof, or equivalent logistics record
Packing list and proof linking the shipped goods to the commercial invoice and customs declaration
Purchase order, sales contract, order confirmation, and delivery records
Evidence of payment or other commercially reliable settlement records where relevant
For intra-Community supplies, customer VAT number validation and transport evidence establishing dispatch to another EU member state
For offshore services, contract, customer business-status evidence, customer establishment and location evidence, service-delivery records, invoice, and reverse-charge wording where applicable

Foreign-exchange or inward-remittance evidence only where required by the applicable customer, banking, accounting, or refund substantiation process; France does not impose a general export-VAT rule requiring an inward-remittance certificate
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: France has no general statutory 180-day foreign-exchange repatriation deadline for export VAT zero-rating. The supplier must be able to prove the legal conditions for the exemption or zero rate and must correct or repay VAT where the evidence is incomplete, contradictory, fabricated, or obtained after the fact. The DGFiP may reassess unpaid VAT, deny input-tax deductions or refunds, recover improperly exempted output VAT, and charge late-payment interest generally at 0.20% per month, subject to statutory rules. Tax penalties can include a 10% surcharge for late payment or filing, 40% for deliberate failure or serious non-compliance, and 80% for fraudulent manoeuvres or abuse of rights; the applicable percentage depends on the conduct and statutory findings. False customs declarations may trigger customs debt, administrative penalties, seizure, and prosecution under the Union Customs Code and French customs law. Intentional tax fraud may result in criminal penalties, including fines and imprisonment under the French Tax Code, in addition to civil tax reassessment. The limitation period and recovery period depend on the relevant VAT, customs, and criminal provisions; records should generally be retained for at least the applicable French VAT and accounting retention periods, commonly ten years for VAT invoices and supporting records.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Banque de France (BdF) in coordination with the Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel et de Résolution (ACPR), the European Central Bank (ECB), and the Direction Générale du Trésor (DG Trésor) under the French Monetary and Financial Code (Code Monétaire et Financier) and EU Treaty provisions on free movement of capital.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The euro is fully convertible for both current-account and capital-account transactions within the EU legal framework. France imposes no exchange controls, no prior-authorization requirements, and no quantitative limits on capital inflows or outflows for a French SAS. Profit and dividend remittance to non-resident shareholders is unrestricted, subject only to standard corporate documentation (audited or approved financial statements, statutory auditor certification if applicable) and to FATCA/CRS beneficial-ownership declarations. There are no remittance hurdles at central-bank level; however, bank-level AML/CFT screening of beneficial owners and source-of-funds evidence remains the de facto compliance gate.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None applicable. France and the euro area do not maintain statutory export-proceeds surrender obligations, mandatory conversion ratios, repatriation timelines, or foreign-currency holding limits for export and cross-border service receipts. An SAS operating a data-pipeline API business may retain receivables in EUR, USD, or any freely convertible currency. Treasury practice should nevertheless implement a disciplined conversion and cash-pooling policy to minimize EUR/USD working-capital exposure and to align with VAT cash-flow timing.

Operational Account, cooperative-model onboarding with local branch authority

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Rating: High feasibility for payment collection, Medium for full treasury concentration, with legal constraints. A French SAS may onboard EU-licensed Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) and Payment Institutions (PIs) such as Qonto, Shine, or Railsbank-type platforms either under ACPR authorization or under the EU payment-services passport. Offshore (non-EEA) digital EMIs are not permitted to hold client funds or provide payment accounts in France without ACPR or cross-border passporting; they may only be used as supplementary collection rails, never as the primary treasury account, and must not accept regulated deposits. Fully regulated ACPR-licensed EMIs with French IBANs are viable for Stripe-payout reconciliation and for converting USDC into EUR via licensed crypto-fiat exchangers; however, the primary operating account should remain with a tier-1 credit institution to satisfy shareholder audit and lender expectations.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Under prevailing French banking practice and ACPR guidance, corporate onboarding typically requires at least one physical in-person or videoconference-recognized interview of the legal representative(s) and UBO(s); however, most tier-1 banks now permit fully remote opening through secure video KYC for French-domiciled directors. Non-resident or 100% foreign-owned shareholders trigger heightened due diligence: a physical meeting at a French branch (or at a French consulate/embassy abroad) is commonly required unless the bank accepts an equivalence letter from a correspondent bank. Directors of an SAS who are non-resident must nevertheless be listed on the Kbis extract and cannot avoid individual identification; a French-resident day-to-day manager (président) materially de-risks onboarding.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: business described as web scraping or mass data collection, perceived as data-privacy or intellectual-property infringement exposure under GDPR (CNIL enforcement) and potentially categorized as high-risk activity by the risk-management committee.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: GDPR/CNIL compliance file: data-protection impact assessment (DPIA), privacy policy, lawful-basis analysis (legitimate interest and Art. 6 records), client/data-source agreements demonstrating that only public-api and lawfully accessible data are processed, robots.txt compliance policy, CNIL registration receipt (if applicable), external counsel legal opinion on contractual and tort liability, and a commercial underwriting presentation mapping the ISIC 6201 software-publishing activity classification to the bank acceptable-activities list.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: non-resident treasury holding company or cross-border shareholders with opaque ownership; UBO identification failure or nominee-shareholder suspicion.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: UBO register extract (Registre des bénéficiaires effectifs) filed within 30 days of constitution, Articles of Association (Statuts) with certified translation, Kbis extract less than 3 months old, passport copies of all directors and UBOs, source-of-funds evidence (shareholder bank statements and tax returns), and proof of economic substance of the foreign holding entity (board minutes, subsidiary registry, audited balance sheet).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: dual payment rails mixing high-volume micro-transaction fiat (Stripe) and cryptocurrency (USDC) settlement, creating an unpredictable cash-flow pattern and potential unlicensed virtual-asset activity.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: AML/CFT governance charter demonstrating that the company is a consumer of crypto as a payment method only and not a VASP (no exchange, custody, or third-party transmission), executed contracts with regulated payment processors (Stripe) and with an ACPR-registered or France-approved Digital Asset Service Provider for USDC-to-EUR conversion, crypto-wallet addresses disclosed and traceability policy (travel-rule compliance where applicable), monthly reconciliation ledger, and clean-source attestation from the crypto on/off-ramp partner.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: high-volume low-ticket international API subscriptions (per-call micro-billing) inconsistent with the declared corporate profile and triggering structured-transaction suspicion.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Public pricing page and rate-card documentation, sample client agreements with multinational counterparties, invoice history and billing cadence, API usage logs mapped to commercial contracts, an external audit letter from the statutory auditor confirming that receivables correspond to bona fide business activities, and projected cash-flow business plan with customer geography breakdown.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: sanctions/embargo exposure from clients located in restricted jurisdictions when using offshore payment endpoints.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Automated sanctions-screening log (EU consolidated list, OFAC SDN, UNSC) with algorithmic coverage procedure, country-blocking policy embedded in the API gateway, geolocation/IP-filtering evidence, contractual prohibition of resale into sanctioned markets, and periodic compliance certification from the chief compliance officer.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant routing for an SAS capital increase or shareholder loan: SWIFT MT103 from the foreign shareholder bank to the French bank with unstructured or structured remittance information (RFB) designating the beneficiary IBAN, the corporate identifier, and the purpose-of-payment code. For FDI-linked equity injections, banks accept EU Balance of Payments purpose code 'M100 - Equity Capital' or the French BDR (Banque de France reporting) code category for direct investment; for intercompany loans, use code 'M11 - Loans and deposits' or 'R.2 - Financial credit'. The Banque de France maintains statistical reporting (cotation) requirements for direct investment flows exceeding EUR 15 million per calendar year or 10% of capital subscribed by non-residents; banks will request the shareholder resolution, subscription agreement, and bank-account-attestation from the notary if a notarized deed is used. All inbound wires must reference the exact SAS legal name and SIREN number to avoid quarantine.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing rails for trade and operational settlements: (1) SWIFT MT103 for cross-border supplier payments and intercompany disbursements, with required purpose codes such as 'PUR - Purchase of software and cloud infrastructure' or 'SPI - Service payment intangibles'; (2) SEPA Credit Transfer (SCT) in EUR within the EU with mandatory ISO 20022 structured remittance; (3) Commercial Letter of Credit (L/C) issued via the French relationship bank only for high-value physical-goods procurement, with Incoterms 2020 and SWIFT MT700 flow; (4) Stripe payout settlement to the operational account via SCT for merchant-acquiring revenues; and (5) segregated USDC conversion flow from the ACPR-compliant VASP partner to the EUR operational account, executed on a same-day T+0/T+1 basis with a full reconciliation file.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable EUR/USD forward contracts (plain vanilla, up to 12-24 months) with a licensed French credit institution or investment firm, requiring ISDA documentation or a bank master agreement and evidence of underlying commercial exposure
EUR/USD and EUR/GBP FX swaps (swap points rollover for working-capital liquidity management in multi-currency accounts)
Euro/USD cross-currency swaps (CCS) for longer-dated shareholder loan or intercompany funding hedges
Zero-cost EUR/USD option collars (range forwards) for protecting export-API revenue margins without upfront premium

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) permissible only for non-convertible or restricted exotic currency pairs (e.g., emerging-market client settlement currencies) where deliverable forward markets are absent; NDFs are not necessary for EUR/USD given full euro convertibility, and would require individual bank credit approval

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual financial statement filing / deposit of annual accounts (dépôt des comptes annuels) with the RCS
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Greffe du Tribunal de Commerce / RCS via the Guichet Unique électronique
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Shareholder approval of annual accounts must occur within 6 months of fiscal year-end (by 30 June for a 31 December year-end); the signed accounts must be filed within 1 month of approval, i.e. ordinarily by 31 July for calendar-year entities.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file exposes the legal representative to a criminal fine of up to EUR 15,000, a court-ordered coercive fine (astreinte), and, after repeated default, administrative strike-off from the RCS; the entity may also be precluded from distributing dividends.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual French corporate income tax return (déclaration de résultats n° 2065 / liasse fiscale)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For calendar-year taxpayers, e-file by 3 May of the following year; for non-calendar fiscal years, file within 90 days of fiscal year close.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty equal to 5% of assessed corporate income tax (10% after formal notice; 40% for deliberately concealed results), plus late-payment interest; repeated non-filing can trigger automatic income assessment and practical closure of the file.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Corporate income tax balance payment (solde d'impôt sur les sociétés - IS)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For calendar-year entities, the balance of corporate income tax is paid by 15 May; for non-calendar year-ends, within 15 days of filing the corporate tax return.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late payment attracts a 5% penalty (10% for repeat offence within 3 years) plus statutory late-payment interest at the monthly rate set by the French tax code; enforced recovery may include attachments and registration of a tax lien.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual payment of local business property contribution (Cotisation Foncière des Entreprises - CFE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: DGFIP / local municipal tax collection authorities
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: The annual CFE assessment notice is payable by 15 December of the tax year; electronic-payment taxpayers are due one day earlier (14 December).
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-payment by 31 December triggers a 10% late-payment increase (20% after formal notice) plus monthly interest; persistent non-payment exposes the business to coercive collection and may disqualify the principal from certain business expense deductions.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A statutory auditor (commissaire aux comptes) is required for a SAS if at the fiscal year-end at least two of the following thresholds are exceeded: total balance sheet assets > EUR 4,000,000; net turnover excluded taxes > EUR 8,000,000; average number of employees > 50. Audit is also mandatory in group/safety/merger situations or when ordered by court or requested by shareholders meeting statutory threshold.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Individual statutory accounts must be prepared under French GAAP (Plan Comptable Général and ANC règlements); consolidated financial statements, if required, are prepared using EU-adopted IFRS.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: France has no standalone annual UBO re-filing requirement. The beneficial-owner declaration (déclaration des bénéficiaires effectifs) is lodged at incorporation and must be updated at the RCS within 30 days of any change in direct or indirect beneficial ownership. In practice, the annual accounts filing season serves as the check-point for confirming that the UBO particulars on file remain accurate, with a corrective declaration filed whenever the prior filing is outdated.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of movements of securities / share register (registre des mouvements de titres)
Register of shareholder decisions and minutes (registre de décisions et procès-verbaux)
Accounting records, minute book and supporting documents kept at the registered office or place of management

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 324 - USD 972 per year (EUR 300-900 excluding VAT) for a standard registered-office/legal-agent domiciliation service in Paris or a main regional commercial centre.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 5,400 - USD 16,200 per engagement (EUR 5,000-15,000 excluding VAT) for an independent statutory audit of a small-to-mid-sized SAS; nil if all audit thresholds are not tripped and no other audit trigger applies.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: France generally has no broad corporate tax holiday. Eligible small companies may apply a 15% rate to the first EUR 42,500 of taxable profit, subject to turnover not exceeding EUR 10 million, fully paid-up capital and at least 75% individual ownership conditions. Qualifying intellectual-property income may be taxed at a separate 10% rate under the net-patent-income regime. The research tax credit is generally 30% of eligible French research expenditure up to EUR 100 million and 5% above that amount. Qualifying innovation expenditure may benefit from the applicable innovation tax-credit regime. Tax incentives require statutory eligibility, supporting records and anti-abuse compliance.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form 2065-SD, corporate income tax return, filed electronically through the EDI-TDFC channel using an approved intermediary or through the French tax administration's professional online services. The return is accompanied by Forms 2050-SD to 2059-SD and applicable sector schedules.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual, with corporate income tax instalments during the year
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The annual return is generally due within three months after the end of the fiscal year. For a fiscal year ending on 31 December, the normal deadline is the second business day after 1 May of the following year. The final corporate income tax balance is generally payable by the 15th day of the fourth month following year-end; for a 31 December year-end, the usual date is 15 May. Tax instalments are generally due on 15 March, 15 June, 15 September and 15 December.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, French SIREN number, registered office, fiscal year dates, legal form, tax office and contact details.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report the French SAS as the taxpayer even where all or part of its share capital is held by non-residents. Use the French registered office and SIREN. Identify any foreign permanent establishment, parent company or tax-consolidation status where requested.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Form 2065-SD, taxable profit or loss section
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable profit or tax loss, corporate income tax due, credits, reductions, instalments and balance payable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include worldwide taxable results of the French-resident SAS, subject to applicable treaty allocation and French exemptions. Do not exclude foreign-source income merely because the shareholders or customers are non-resident.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation from accounting profit or loss to taxable profit or loss, including non-deductible expenses, exempt income, tax adjustments, depreciation differences and provisions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Add back expenses that fail French deductibility rules, including unsupported related-party charges, excessive interest, non-business expenditure and penalties. Document the tax treatment of foreign exchange, platform fees, software costs, data acquisition and cloud infrastructure.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tracking of tax losses, loss carryforwards, carryback claims and utilization against current-year taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Maintain detailed schedules supporting French tax losses and any continuity of business. Loss utilization is subject to the French annual limitation, generally EUR 1 million plus 50% of the portion of current-year profit exceeding EUR 1 million. French losses are not freely transferable to a foreign parent.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of taxable income and calculation of corporate income tax, including relevant tax credits and withholding tax offsets.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only credits legally available to the SAS and retain certificates for foreign tax, withholding and eligible expenditure. Treaty relief does not automatically convert foreign withholding into a French tax credit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Balance sheet, income statement and accounting disclosures.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use French statutory accounts or accounts reconciled to French tax rules. Disclose related-party balances, shareholder loans, foreign accounts and material intercompany positions consistently with the transfer-pricing file.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital gains and losses, including disposals of fixed assets, securities and certain intellectual-property assets.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify asset location, legal owner, acquisition basis, disposal proceeds and any treaty allocation. Software, databases, domain names and intellectual-property rights require separate classification.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital gains and losses subject to special tax treatment and calculation of net amounts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply French rules to gains realized by the French SAS. Do not treat a shareholder-level disposal of SAS shares as a company-level gain.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign tax credits and foreign-source income, where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report foreign withholding or foreign taxes only where the legal conditions for a French credit or deduction are satisfied. Retain foreign tax certificates and apply treaty limitations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Statement of certain deductible expenses, including specified commissions, brokerage, fees and similar payments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose qualifying payments to foreign intermediaries and related parties where the form applies. Preserve contracts, invoices, beneficial-owner information and evidence of actual services.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Annual simplified transfer-pricing declaration, where the statutory threshold or related-party conditions are met.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report the nature, amount and jurisdiction of cross-border controlled transactions. Ensure consistency with the local file, master file, statutory accounts and customs valuation records.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Form 2571-SD and corporate tax instalment records
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Corporate income tax instalment payments and payment references.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident shareholder does not remove the French SAS's obligation to pay instalments. Verify bank mandates, payment references and any exemption or reduced instalment entitlement.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late or missing filing may trigger a 10% surcharge, increased to 40% in cases involving formal notice and potentially 80% in fraudulent or abusive circumstances. Late payment generally attracts a 5% payment surcharge plus late interest, ordinarily 0.20% per month, subject to statutory exceptions and current administrative rules. Underpayment may also produce tax reassessment, interest, penalties for intentional misconduct and criminal referral for fraud.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Corporate income tax instalments and balance payment through the French tax administration's professional online account or approved electronic payment channel.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Quarterly instalments and annual balancing payment
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Instalments are generally due on the 15th of March, June, September and December. The final balance is generally due by the 15th day of the fourth month after fiscal year-end.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxpayer identification and payment allocation data.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the SAS SIREN and tax account, not the foreign parent's tax identification number.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Prior-year or estimated current-year corporate income tax liability used to calculate instalments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Recalculate where the prior-year liability is not representative, including start-up losses, cessation, tax-group changes or major business restructuring.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Current-year tax liability less instalments, credits and legally available offsets.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reconcile the payment to Form 2065 and the filed financial statements. Interest and penalties can arise if the balance is materially underpaid.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late payment generally results in a 5% surcharge and late-payment interest. Repeated or material payment default may lead to formal notices, enforced collection, bank account seizure, director-liability proceedings in exceptional cases and criminal action where fraud is established.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% domestic withholding tax generally applies to dividends and similar distributions paid by a French company to a non-resident beneficial owner, subject to exemptions, treaty relief and anti-abuse rules. A qualifying EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive exemption may reduce the rate to 0%, commonly requiring at least 10% ownership, a qualifying corporate recipient, minimum holding-period conditions or a holding commitment, subject-to-tax status and anti-abuse compliance.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: Before payment, obtain a valid certificate of tax residence from the beneficial owner and establish beneficial ownership, treaty eligibility, minimum holding, limitation-on-benefits or principal-purpose-test compliance and absence of conduit arrangements. Apply the treaty rate only where French procedural conditions are met. Depending on the payment and recipient, relief may be obtained at source using the applicable French forms, including Form 5000 and relevant annexes, or by withholding at the domestic rate and filing a refund claim with the French tax administration. Retain the residence certificate, corporate documents, ownership chart, board resolutions, payment records, anti-abuse analysis and evidence of recipient taxation. Treaty relief is unavailable to a nominee, conduit or entity lacking economic substance.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: French-source royalties paid to non-residents are generally subject to 25% withholding, with a potential 75% rate for payments to non-cooperative jurisdictions or territories and other statutory anti-abuse cases. Applicable tax treaties commonly reduce royalty withholding to 0%, 5%, 8%, 10% or another specified rate. Ordinary interest paid by a French company to a non-resident is generally not subject to French withholding under domestic law, although specific financial products, non-cooperative-jurisdiction payments, anti-abuse provisions and beneficial-owner rules can produce withholding. Treaties commonly provide 0% to 10% maximum interest rates. Payments for software, databases, technical access or data rights must be classified carefully because a royalty, service fee or business-profit characterization may produce different outcomes.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: EUR 400,000,000: French master-file and local-file documentation requirements generally apply to entities or French tax groups meeting the EUR 400 million turnover or gross-assets threshold, or linked to an entity or group meeting the threshold. A separate annual simplified transfer-pricing declaration, Form 2257-SD, generally applies where the French entity or group has turnover or gross assets of at least EUR 50 million, or is linked to an entity meeting that threshold, subject to statutory conditions. Documentation may be requested below the thresholds where the tax administration challenges pricing.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: France does not operate a single standalone Economic Substance Regulations regime equivalent to certain offshore jurisdictions. Economic substance is nevertheless required in practice through the arm's-length principle, beneficial-ownership requirements, general anti-abuse doctrine, abuse-of-law rules, controlled-foreign-company rules, interest-limitation rules, permanent-establishment principles, anti-hybrid rules, EU ATAD measures and principal-purpose-test treaty provisions. A French SAS providing scraping, data-pipeline or proxy API services should maintain French decision-making, personnel or demonstrable outsourced operational control, technical capability, contracts, risk management, accounting records, customer-service functions and commercially credible remuneration. An entity with nominal directors, no operational capacity and pass-through invoicing is exposed to recharacterization, denial of deductions, withholding-tax disputes and permanent-establishment or beneficial-ownership challenges.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Concealing revenue from API subscriptions, cryptocurrency receipts or foreign payment processors; fabricating expenses; maintaining parallel accounts; falsifying invoices; or deliberately omitting taxable transactions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax reassessment, late interest, penalties generally ranging from 40% for intentional misconduct to 80% for fraudulent maneuvers or abusive arrangements, and criminal tax-fraud sanctions that can include imprisonment of up to 5 years and a fine of up to EUR 500,000. Aggravated cases, including organized fraud or use of accounts or entities in certain jurisdictions, may carry up to 7 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to EUR 3 million, subject to statutory conditions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face criminal liability where they personally participate in fraud. In addition, a director may be declared jointly liable for tax debts under Article L267 of the French Tax Procedures Book where fraudulent maneuvers or serious and repeated non-compliance make recovery impossible. Travel restrictions are not an automatic tax sanction but may arise from judicial proceedings or enforcement measures. Civil restitution, asset seizure and professional disqualification may also apply.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company, Beneficial Ownership and Substance Failure
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the SAS as a conduit for foreign affiliates, routing royalties or service fees through an entity with no personnel or decision-making, nominee ownership, circular payments or treaty-shopping structures lacking commercial purpose.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Denial of treaty benefits, recharacterization of payments, withholding at domestic or aggravated rates, denial of deductions, abuse-of-law penalties, reassessment and interest. Anti-abuse penalties may reach 80% where fraudulent or abusive conduct is established.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may incur civil and criminal exposure for knowingly implementing sham arrangements or false records. Joint tax-debt liability is possible under Article L267 where the statutory conditions are met; insolvency-related management liability may also arise if misconduct contributes to insufficient assets.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length fees for data, software, scraping infrastructure, proxy capacity, marketing, management or financing; shifting profits to a low-tax affiliate; or failing to document controlled transactions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Reassessment under French transfer-pricing rules, denial of deductions, withholding-tax exposure, late interest, 40% or 80% penalties depending on conduct, and a penalty for missing or materially defective transfer-pricing documentation that can be substantial and is linked to reassessed profits or statutory amounts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not automatically liable for an ordinary pricing adjustment, but personal liability may arise for intentional concealment, false documentation, obstruction, fraudulent accounting or conduct causing unrecoverable tax debt.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Accepting USDC or other crypto-assets without transaction monitoring, customer identification, sanctions screening, source-of-funds checks, suspicious-transaction escalation and reliable euro valuation; using unregistered exchange or custody providers; or disguising crypto proceeds as ordinary sales.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax reassessment and penalties for unreported income, accounting penalties, freezing or seizure of assets, and AML sanctions. Money laundering can carry up to 5 years' imprisonment and a EUR 375,000 fine, with aggravated penalties potentially reaching 10 years and EUR 750,000 where statutory conditions apply. Regulated-activity breaches may result in administrative or criminal sanctions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and beneficial owners may be personally prosecuted for knowingly facilitating laundering, sanctions evasion or unlicensed financial activity. Civil confiscation, asset seizure, management bans and judicial restrictions may apply; travel bans are case-specific and not automatic.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: False Invoicing and Undocumented Intercompany Services
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Issuing or receiving invoices for services that were not performed, backdating agreements, using generic descriptions for data or software services, or deducting foreign charges without proof of benefit and delivery.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Denial of deductions, corporate tax reassessment, VAT reassessment where applicable, penalties for deliberate or fraudulent conduct, and possible criminal prosecution for accounting or tax fraud.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: A director who authorizes or knowingly approves fictitious invoices may face criminal liability, personal civil claims, tax-debt solidarity in exceptional statutory circumstances and insolvency-related liability.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Unlawful Web Scraping, Data Protection and Cybersecurity
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Scraping personal data without a lawful basis, ignoring robots.txt or contractual access restrictions where legally relevant, bypassing authentication or technical controls, violating database rights, reselling protected content, or failing to implement GDPR security and transparency measures.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative orders, processing restrictions, data deletion, contractual damages, intellectual-property or database-right claims and GDPR fines of up to EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the relevant infringements. Unauthorized access to an automated data-processing system may also trigger criminal sanctions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face personal criminal exposure for intentional unauthorized access, unlawful data processing or obstruction, as well as civil claims where personal fault is established. Corporate tax deductions may be challenged if expenditure relates to unlawful conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Maintain Accounting and Corporate Records
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to keep French-compliant accounts, omitting crypto transactions, mixing shareholder and company funds, failing to preserve contracts and transfer-pricing evidence, or refusing to produce records during a tax audit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax reassessment based on estimated income, reversal of deductions, accounting and tax penalties, rejection of claims, enforced collection and potential criminal consequences for obstruction or fraudulent accounting.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: The president and other de facto managers may be liable for serious management failures, fraudulent accounting, insolvency misconduct and unrecoverable tax debts. A corporate veil is not ordinarily pierced solely because of ownership, but personal liability increases materially where the company is used as an instrument of fraud.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Late Filing, Late Payment and Repeated Non-Compliance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Missing the Form 2065 deadline, failing to pay instalments, submitting materially incomplete schedules, or repeatedly ignoring tax-authority notices.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Generally a 10% late-filing surcharge, a 5% late-payment surcharge and late interest of 0.20% per month, with higher penalties after formal notice or where deliberate or fraudulent conduct is established. Repeated failures may trigger audit escalation and enforced recovery.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Ordinary late filing does not automatically create director liability. Serious and repeated non-compliance combined with fraudulent maneuvers can support Article L267 tax-debt solidarity and management-liability proceedings.
